title: Magic Patterns Alternatives That Are Actually Better
summary: Magic Patterns alternatives for PMs and designers, compared on design-system import, editable Figma export, real code and credit costs.
body_markdown:
Key takeaways:


- Three of the nine Magic Patterns alternatives after ours export to Figma on a free plan: MagicPath (3 exports a month), Polymet (per its docs) and Figr.
- Of those nine, three have no native Figma export (Claude Design, Subframe and v0), and Awesomic documents none.
- Magic Patterns' own Figma export starts on Starter, $17 a seat a month billed annually per its pricing FAQ.
- Its docs price a full page or flow (11 to 20 versions, on Claude Opus 5.5) at about 400 credits, so Starter's 1,000 monthly credits cover about two and a half (our arithmetic).


Magic Patterns alternatives are worth a look when a prototype has to match your real product and go somewhere after the demo: into Figma as layers a designer can keep editing, and into a repo as code an engineer will keep. Magic Patterns turns a prompt into a React front end, which is enough for a demo.


The friction starts with your design system and the trip back to Figma. So "better" here means better at one job: your design system in, editable Figma and real code out, for PMs and product designers. No tool wins everywhere, so each entry says where it wins.


It's our product, so[Awesomic](https://www.awesomic.com/) sits first, though it documents no Figma export: it's here for teams whose prototype has to become a live site. The six alternatives to Magic Patterns that do export come next, ordered by the cheapest plan with that export on annual billing, ties among the three free ones broken by the cheapest paid plan.


The three with no native Figma export close the list, ordered by lowest paid price. We re-read prices on each vendor's site on November 13, 2026.


## Why design-system teams look past Magic Patterns


Magic Patterns hasn't stood still. MagicOS (October 13, 2026) added an infinite canvas, parallel agent threads, voice, and import and export with your codebase, Claude Design and Figma, and an Edit mode followed on October 30. The gaps are in how your system gets in and how work gets out.


Magic Patterns publishes no plan gate for importing your system. You can import a GitHub repo, a zipped code folder, a website URL (colors, fonts and styles, not components) or a` .fig` file yourself. An npm package takes a guided call per its docs, though its design-systems page says you can connect one yourself, and the pricing page lists "Custom import design system" under Enterprise.


On the way out, you get a front end only: React 18, TypeScript and Tailwind v3 by default, with "no API calls, no auth, no backend". A[Reddit thread in r/uxwriting](https://www.reddit.com/r/uxwriting/comments/1suoe03/for_those_whose_teams_are_increasingly_using/) from April 2026 adds an anecdote: a UX writer whose team uses Magic Patterns most said the "final 10%" hurts.


That writer described about two minutes per prompt to test one copy change, in a post that predates Edit mode. Their workaround was exporting to Figma and editing there, though they called Figma exports from AI tools "usually at least a little wonky". If you haven't settled on AI generation at all, weigh it against other[prototyping tools](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/prototyping-tools) first.


## The best Magic Patterns alternatives, compared


Here's the shortlist, with the column this article turns on at the end.


Awesomic brings AI agents and vetted experts into one app. Start with a prompt to build a website, app, campaign, deck or video, then switch models or bring in a vetted expert without losing the project context. AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


Six tools after ours send work to Figma, three of them on a free plan, though what lands there varies by tool.


### 1. Awesomic


**Best for:** Turning a prototype into a live site


**Overview:** Magic Patterns hands you a front end with no backend. In Awesomic, every project gets its own cloud computer, where agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode) install and run real programs, so a prototype can become a working site that doesn't depend on your machine.


Inside that project, Brand memory keeps one record of your brand, files and decisions, 200+ templates give you a start, and a finished page goes live at a link in one click. The model labs we route work to can't train on your files. Under our Terms, Awesomic may still use de-identified content to train and improve its own AI, and opting out applies from that point forward.


Figma is among more than 1,000 apps you can connect, though no export into it is documented. On a separate expert plan, a screen that needs a designer's eye goes from the same chat to one of our 200+ vetted experts, who cover 30+ skill sets.


**Key features:**


- Parallel agents on one project's files, one chat each.
- Models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI billed together; bring a Claude or Codex plan if you like.
- Per-person access, approved models and budgets for admins.
- Open it in a browser, the Mac, Windows or Linux desktop app, or the iPhone and Android apps.


**Pricing:** Light is $19 per person per month, which is also that person's monthly AI budget. The same agents and models come on Basic, Pro and Studio, which lift the budget to $99, $199 and $499, and unspent budget resets monthly.


Designers come on separate expert plans. Graphic Pack, at $1,799 a month, buys a part-time designer for ads, emails, packaging, print and everyday graphics. For screens or a site, look at All-in-One, at $3,219 a month, which adds copywriting, no-code development and quality checks, or a Dedicated expert quoted on a call. Each includes one Light seat.


For current Awesomic plans and capabilities, see[the pricing page](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**Pros:** A real site instead of a mock, Brand memory, one-click publish, vetted designers


**Cons:** AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**How to start using it:**


1. Put each person who'll prompt on Light.
2. Start a project from a template or a prompt.
3. Add your brand rules to the project's files (Brand memory).
4. Connect GitHub, Slack or other apps.
5. Publish to a live link, then add an expert plan if needed.


**Why it's a good Magic Patterns alternative:** It goes past the prototype: agents publish the real site, and a vetted designer can finish it.


**Final verdict:** Choose Awesomic when the prototype has to ship as a real site with a designer for the finish. If you need editable Figma round trips on your library, Figr fits better.


[Get started](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) on the Light plan.


### 2. MagicPath


**Overview:** MagicPath ("The visual layer for all your agent work") has run parallel designer agents on one canvas since version 2.0 in May 2026. A pasted Figma frame becomes React with no AI or credits spent, and your system comes in as a Tailwind config, a DESIGN.md, a web URL or CSS.


**Key features:**


- "Copy to Figma" as editable layers, unlimited from Builder.
- React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind, as a ZIP or opened in Cursor.


**Pricing:** Free gives 20 credits a day, up to 120 a month, with 3 Figma exports a month. Builder is $7 a month billed annually, or $10 monthly, and Pro is $21 billed annually, or $30 monthly, with a 600-credit pack; credits don't roll over.


**Pros:** Editable export on Free, credit-free Figma-to-React


**Cons:** 120 credits a month on Free, repo components need Cursor, Codex or a Claude Code plugin, its pricing page and docs disagree on Builder's Figma imports, best on desktop


**Where it beats Magic Patterns:** Editable Figma export comes on the free plan, where Magic Patterns needs Starter.


**Final verdict:** Pick MagicPath for unlimited editable exports on the cheapest paid plan here, if a Tailwind config holds your system.


### 3. Polymet


**Overview:** Polymet ("AI product designer, at your service.") publishes its prices in its docs, not on a pricing page, and its August 10, 2026 changelog introduced the plans. Its homepage lists GitHub, public and private npm packages and Storybook as sources, though its docs describe only GitHub and ZIP import and don't mention npm or Storybook. Figma component import keeps variants.


**Key features:**


- Figma export through an Export ID pasted into its plugin.
- React and Tailwind, with a ZIP download on paid plans.
- Two-way GitHub sync with branches, plus Polymet MCP.


**Pricing:** Free gives every org 500 credits every 30 days, and Pro is $25 a month, or $250 a year, for 1,000 credits, scaling up in twelve sizes. Team starts at $50 a month, and its changelog says "preview and publishing stay free on every plan", while code export needs a paid plan.


**Pros:** Free Figma export and publishing, private npm packages on its source list, variants kept on import


**Cons:** No standalone pricing page, docs that don't mention npm or Storybook, its FAQ says it may train on your content unless you opt out (Enterprise is opted out by default)


**The case for it:** Per its homepage, an npm package comes in without the call Magic Patterns requires.


**Final verdict:** Try Polymet if your system ships as an npm package.


### 4. Figr


**Overview:** Figr ("Design with an AI that already understands your product") pulls context from PRDs, recordings, analytics notes and a Chrome extension that captures your live product. Design systems come in through a Figma plugin, a Storybook MCP server, a public npm package, a GitHub repo, or CSS and token files.


**Key features:**


- Figma export on every plan, as editable auto-layout frames mapped to your variables.
- Library components placed as instances when you export into the library file.
- React or Angular built with your components, plus Figr MCP for coding agents.


**Pricing:** Free has 10 credits a month and a "Limited Design System". Starter is $32 a month billed yearly, or $39 monthly, for 200 credits and 3 design systems, and Max is $124 billed yearly, or $149 monthly, for 1,000 shared credits and up to 3 seats.


**Pros:** Exports mapped to your library, edge-case and state mapping


**Cons:** 10 credits a month on Free, one seat on Starter, its pages disagree on credit rollover


**Why it's a strong Magic Patterns alternative:** Exports onto your own variables and library come on every plan, though Free's design system is limited.


**Final verdict:** Start with Figr if your system lives in a Figma library.


### 5. Figma Make


**Overview:** Figma Make ("Prototype. Polish. Ship.") works inside Figma, so its Make kits read the npm packages, published library variables and styles, and guidelines your team already has. Layers copied back from a preview on a paid plan stay editable and bind to variables in the file, but "aren't interactive" and have no link to the Make file.


**Key features:**


- Make kits for Full seats on paid plans.
- React and TypeScript, with a ZIP download for Full or Dev seats.


**Pricing:** Figma's free Starter plan allows 150 AI credits in a day and 500 in a month. On Professional, a Full seat runs $16 a month billed annually, or $20 monthly, with 3,000 credits a month.


**Pros:** Your published library is already in reach, no new vendor on Full seats


**Cons:** Make kits need a Full seat on a paid plan, credits shared across all Figma AI with no rollover, non-interactive copies


**When it's the better pick:** Your whole team already works in Figma on Full seats.


**Final verdict:** Choose Figma Make to stay in one app, if non-interactive copies back are enough.


### 6. UX Pilot


**Overview:** UX Pilot ("Create UI that's worth building on") drafts whole multi-screen flows and adds predictive heatmaps. Its plan page lists "Import your full design system" under Enterprise, while its design-system page describes starting from a website, a Figma file (beta), a GitHub repo, local code or a DESIGN.md, so check what your plan covers.


**Key features:**


- Editable Figma export with auto layout from Pro, and component import on every plan.
- HTML and CSS or a React project, with GitHub sync.


**Pricing:** Free covers up to 13 screens and 80 credits a day. Pro is $19 a month billed annually, with $29 listed monthly, for 125 screens and 750 credits, and Teams is $31 per user billed annually, with $39 listed monthly.


**Pros:** Whole multi-screen flows, editable export with auto layout, GitHub sync


**Cons:** Real-time collaboration only on Teams, plan details that shift


**Where it pulls ahead:** Component import works on Free, and heatmaps are built in, while Magic Patterns sends npm libraries to a guided setup.


**Final verdict:** Pick UX Pilot for flow-level drafts, and budget for Pro if work has to reach Figma.


### 7. Anima


**Overview:** Anima ("AI with an Eye for Design") imports selected Figma components into a Playground from Starter up, where they run as a live Storybook with variants, states and props. Without a library, it matches a brand from a URL or a Design.md, and it writes HTML or React.


**Key features:**


- "Copy to Figma" export with auto layout and editable layers, at 1 chat credit each.
- Anima MCP for Claude Code, Cursor or Copilot.


**Pricing:** Free gives 5 chat messages and 5 code generations a month. Starter is $20 a seat billed annually, or $25 monthly, for 100 messages and 50 code generations, and Pro is $40 billed annually, or $50 monthly.


**Pros:** Editable export with auto layout, your components as live code


**Cons:** Only 5 messages and 5 code generations on Free, export and import start at Starter, "Playgrounds are public by default"


**Its edge over Magic Patterns:** Your Figma components become working code, and the export back keeps auto layout.


**Final verdict:** Choose Anima if your system lives in Figma components, and check each Playground's visibility.


### 8. Claude Design


**Overview:** Claude Design ("Design your idea with Claude") comes with every Claude plan, Free too. It takes one or several design systems from a GitHub repo, design files or uploads, and` /design-sync` in Claude Code reads React tokens and components.


**Key features:**


- Exports to .zip, PDF, PPTX, Google Slides or HTML, or sends to Canva, Lovable, v0 and Vercel.
- Hands off to Claude Code.


**Pricing:** Claude Pro is $17 a month on annual billing, or $20 monthly, and Max and Ultra cost $100 and $200. Claude Design shares your Claude usage limits, so heavy design work can leave it "unavailable until your limits reset".


**Pros:** No extra subscription on a Claude plan, several systems per account, a path to Claude Code


**Cons:** No native Figma export (Figma files are input only), no version history yet, multi-person editing described as basic


**Better than Magic Patterns for:** Teams whose next step is Claude Code rather than a Figma file.


**Final verdict:** Use Claude Design if you already live in Claude and nothing has to go back to Figma.


### 9. Subframe


**Overview:** Subframe ("Design & build in one tool.") generates React and Tailwind deterministically. Its desktop app imports your theme, components and icons from your codebase, and tokens come from a Tailwind config, CSS or JSON. Figma is import only, through PNG paste and token import.


**Key features:**


- ` npx @subframe/cli sync` into your repo, plus MCP for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.
- Web access and desktop apps for macOS and Windows.


**Pricing:** Free includes 1 project, unlimited viewers and editors, 3,000 welcome credits per team that don't expire, a monthly allocation per seat and 24 hours of version history. Pro is $20 per editor a month.


**Pros:** Deterministic code, unlimited viewers and editors on Free, components synced by CLI


**Cons:** One-way sync ("Local changes to synced files will be overwritten"), works best with React, codebase workflows need the desktop app


**Where it earns its spot:** The same design always yields the same React code.


**Final verdict:** Choose Subframe when engineering, not Figma, is where the work has to land.


### 10. v0


**Overview:** v0 from Vercel ("What do you want to create?") builds in Next.js, React, Tailwind and shadcn. Design Systems 2.0 takes an npm package or` .tgz` , GitHub repos, Storybook and docs links, and Figma frames, then saves the system as a team skill.


**Key features:**


- Design Mode, GitHub sync and Vercel deploy on Free.
- Figma frame import on paid plans.


**Pricing:** Free comes with $5 in one-time credits and a cap of 7 messages daily. Plus costs $30 and Business $100, each per user per month.


**Pros:** npm and Storybook routes in one place, a branch per chat, deploys to Vercel


**Cons:** No Figma export, Figma import paywalled, 7 messages a day on Free, token-priced credits


**What it gets right:** An npm package or Storybook comes in self-serve, where Magic Patterns puts npm on a call.


**Final verdict:** Pick v0 if your product runs on Next.js and shadcn and Figma only feeds it frames.


## Tools we didn't include


UXPin uses your React components too and doesn't list a Figma export, and three tools without one already close this list. Lovable builds full-stack apps and takes Figma only as an import. Banani's pages contradict each other on which plan exports to Figma.


Google Stitch is still in beta with no published price, and[our Google Stitch roundup](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/google-stitch-alternatives) covers the tools people weigh against it. Uizard exports images, SVG or PDF, plus CSS or React per component, but has no native Figma export, so it would be a fourth tool without one.


## What each tool accepts as your design system


Sticking to a design system is a known weak spot for AI prototypes. In a CHIWORK 2026 study,[Li and colleagues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.10652) ran interviews with 22 product team members, 9 of them UX/UI designers, and summed up what the designers reported as "weaker adherence to design systems".


One participant, P22, said: "It's fine if I just send a screenshot, but once I try to go beyond that, like using design libraries. it doesn't really follow them." So the import route matters more than the demo, and here's what each tool takes.


Tool From code From Figma Notes and plan gates

Whichever route fits, an import is only as good as the system behind it, so settle[what your design system covers](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/design-system) before you pay a tool to read it.


## What actually lands in Figma when you export


"Figma export" means different things across these Magic Patterns alternatives, and the difference decides whether a designer can keep working. Here's what Magic Patterns and the nine tools after ours say arrives:


- Figr exports editable auto-layout frames mapped to your variables, as library instances if you export into the library file itself.
- MagicPath, Anima and UX Pilot copy editable layers into Figma, Anima and UX Pilot with auto layout.
- Figma Make's copies stay editable and bind to the file's variables, but lose interactivity and any link to the Make file.
- Magic Patterns' docs don't say whether pasted layers keep interactivity or map to variables.
- Polymet exports through its plugin, and its docs say the layers arrive editable but not whether they map to variables, so test it.
- Claude Design, Subframe and v0 have no native Figma export.


Layers that aren't tied to your library still work as a reference, but someone then swaps your components in by hand. In a[Reddit thread in r/UXDesign](https://www.reddit.com/r/UXDesign/comments/1njlk0h/how_to_manage_pms_ai_prototyping_in_a_startup/) , a designer said developers treat their final Figma output as a wireframe, because the file is "essentially empty, no design systems or components that resemble what we have on production".


It's one anecdote, but it's the outcome a mapped export is meant to prevent. If staying inside Figma matters more,[our Figma Make roundup](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/figma-make-alternatives) weighs the trade-off for teams who'd rather not add a tool.


## What a prototype costs in credits


Plan prices tell you little here, because every tool meters generation differently. Magic Patterns' docs list about 400 credits on Claude Opus 5.5 when a full page or flow takes 11 to 20 versions, and about 950 for a substantial project of 21 to 50.


At Starter's monthly price of $20 per 1,000 credits, or $0.02 a credit, that's about $8 and about $19 (our arithmetic). Treat both as estimates: the docs say bigger tasks use more credits, and each reply shows what it cost. The table pairs each tool's entry paid plan with the catch to check before you pay.


For a first generation, Magic Patterns' docs list 70 credits and Figr's pricing page 5 to 6 per full web page, measured differently, so treat neither as a per-screen price.


## Handing a prototype to engineering


Handoff trouble is older than AI prototyping. In a systematic review of 45 papers published since 2004, in Proc. ACM Hum.-Comput. Interact. (CSCW),[Zhang and colleagues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.11748) describe developers who "occasionally modify designers' work after the designer-developer handoff without proper communication with designers".


Code built on your real components gives engineers less of that rework, and the tools differ in how it reaches them. Magic Patterns syncs two ways with a new GitHub repo, and Polymet's two-way sync works with branches.


v0 opens a Git branch per chat, while Subframe's CLI pushes components one way and overwrites local edits. Figr, Anima, Polymet and Subframe connect to coding agents over MCP, as Magic Patterns does. Ask your engineers which they'd rather receive before you pick.


## Mistakes that make an AI prototype harder to hand off


The first mistake is testing with a screenshot. P22's complaint was that tools follow a screenshot but not a library, so run your trial on a screen with real components, tokens, states and copy.


Reading an editable Figma export as finished is the next trap. Ask whether layers keep auto layout, map to your variables and arrive as library instances, because a copy that looks right can still need rebuilding on your components.


Skipping the data terms is the last one. Polymet's FAQ says your content may be used for training unless you opt out, and Anima's Playgrounds are public by default, which matters for screens of a product you haven't launched. Check every vendor's terms, ours too.


## Picking the right Magic Patterns alternative for your team


Start with where your design system lives. If it's a Figma library and work has to come back mapped to it, try Figr first, then Anima for components running as a live Storybook, or Figma Make if you're already on Full seats.


If the system lives in code, v0 takes npm and Storybook directly, Polymet's homepage lists both, and Subframe gives React teams deterministic output synced by CLI. Claude Design costs nothing extra if you pay for Claude.


On a tight budget, MagicPath's Builder puts unlimited Figma exports at $7 a month billed annually, and PMs drafting whole flows should look at UX Pilot. If Uizard is on your list too,[our Uizard roundup](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/uizard-alternatives) compares where teams go from it.


## Run the same screen through two tools this week


Pick one screen your team ships often, built from real components. Run it through Magic Patterns and through the alternative that matches where your system lives, then export both to Figma and to code.


Count four things: credits spent, layers rebuilt, code an engineer kept, and time spent on copy edits. The tool that wins on your own screen is the better one for you. If the winner still needs a designer to make it a finished site, our[web design team](https://www.awesomic.com/web-design) can take it from the prototype.


## FAQ


### Is there a free Magic Patterns alternative that exports to Figma?


Yes, three. MagicPath's Free plan includes 3 Figma exports a month on 20 credits a day. Polymet's docs list Figma export on every plan, with 500 credits every 30 days, and Figr exports on every plan, including Free's 10 credits a month.


### Which alternatives to Magic Patterns work best with a Figma library?


Figr is the closest fit: it reads your library through a Figma plugin and exports frames mapped to your variables, placing components as instances when the export lands in the library file. Anima turns selected Figma components into a live Storybook from Starter, and Figma Make reads published library variables and styles for Full seats on paid plans.


### Can Magic Patterns import my design system?


Yes. You can bring in a repo from GitHub, a zipped folder of code, a` .fig` upload or a website URL yourself, while npm packages need a guided setup on a call, and Enterprise adds a custom import.


### Which Magic Patterns alternatives give engineers code they can keep?


v0 writes Next.js and shadcn code with a Git branch per chat, and Polymet syncs both ways with GitHub, branches included. Subframe pushes React components into your repo by CLI, and Figr writes React or Angular with your own components.


### What if the prototype has to become a native mobile app?


All nine alternatives after ours write web code: React, Angular, HTML or Next.js. If an app store is the goal, a no-code mobile builder fits better, and[our Adalo alternatives roundup](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/adalo-alternatives) compares those.
